Italy: Intesa opens its roughly €34.5 billion offer for Monte dei Paschi, which the Siena board calls "fair" without recommending it

Since 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, November 24, Monte dei Paschi (MPS) shareholders can tender their shares to the offer from Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest bank. The offer, valued at about €34.5 billion by Reuters, runs until January 22. The MPS board calls it "fair" but does not recommend it [1][2][4].
For each MPS share tendered, Intesa pays €1.25 in cash and 1.664 new Intesa shares. The exchange ratio was raised to offset the 22-cent interim dividend Intesa paid on November 23 [2].
The timetable, set with Borsa Italiana, runs from 8:30 a.m. on November 24 to 5:30 p.m. on January 22, 2027, unless extended; payment is scheduled for January 29 [2].
Intesa is targeting 66.67% of MPS's capital, but can settle for 50% plus one share; below that, the offer lapses [3].

On November 20, the MPS board, advised by UBS and Bank of America, unanimously found the price financially "congruous", while saying it "does not fully reflect" the group's value and prospects; it recommends neither accepting nor rejecting [4][5][6].

The board notes that the premium offered, €4.2 billion, represents only about 27% of the savings expected from the merger [6]. Director Corrado Passera resigned in the middle of the meeting, in "strong disagreement" with the offer [5].
Milan broker Equita, by contrast, considers the financial terms "fully" fair [7].
MPS's largest shareholder, the holding company Delfin (17.6%), has committed to tender its shares [8].
Key takeaway: barring a surprise, MPS, rescued by the state in 2017, will come under Intesa's control, and with it Mediobanca, which MPS swallowed in 2025 [8][13][15].

Intesa launched the offer in June, without MPS's agreement, for €30.6 billion [11]. MPS first judged it too low and tried to defend itself through other deals [9]. But on October 29, its shareholders rejected the defense plan of CEO Luigi Lovaglio, who insisted the game "was not over" [9].
To reassure competition authorities, Intesa has promised to sell a separate bank grouping about 635 MPS branches to insurer Unipol, for €3 billion to €3.5 billion in cash [10].
The exact value of the deal depends on Intesa's share price, since most of it is paid in shares: €30.6 billion at the announcement, about €34.5 billion today according to Reuters [4][11].

If you are a customer of MPS or of a bank bought by Unipol, nothing changes on your account for now. But banks in Europe are consolidating: fewer competitors can, over time, push up the fees and rates you are offered.

How it works: an offer paid in shares and cash

In a public purchase and exchange offer, the buyer pays mostly with its own shares, issued for the occasion, plus some cash. Here, each MPS share entitles its holder to 1.664 Intesa shares and €1.25 [2]. The value of the offer therefore moves every day with Intesa's share price: €30.6 billion in June, about €34.5 billion according to Reuters in late November [4][11]. MPS shareholders compare this package with MPS's market share price: if the package is worth more, they have an incentive to tender. The 66.67% threshold matters because it lets the holder pass major decisions at shareholder meetings on its own; Intesa has allowed itself to go down to 50% plus one share, which gives simple control [3].

Lebanon: five weeks before UN peacekeepers leave, Europe is sending only a training mission, far from the Israeli border

The mandate of UNIFIL, the UN force in southern Lebanon, ends on December 31. To succeed it, the European Union is preparing a mission to train the Lebanese army, limited to the area north of the Litani River, with no peacekeeping force. On Tuesday, November 24, new Israeli strikes were still hitting the south [1][2][5][7].

UNIFIL will remain fully operational until December 31, 2026, then begin its withdrawal on January 1, 2027, its spokesperson confirmed [5]. French minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the drawdown will run until the end of 2027 [9].

On October 12, the 27 EU member states created the EUSM Lebanon mission, for three years. It is to train the Lebanese army and internal security forces, including for security at the port of Beirut [1].

On November 18, the German government approved sending up to 15 police and customs officers, and a small number of military personnel to train the Lebanese navy. Berlin specifies that the area of operations is limited to territory north of the Litani [2]. Austria adopted its own framework on November 11 [3].

Meeting in Paris on November 9 and 10, G7 foreign ministers said it was necessary to "avoid a security vacuum", but Jean-Noël Barrot acknowledged there was "no breakthrough" on what would replace UNIFIL [4].

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun prefers an extension of UNIFIL or of its operations in 2027. Failing that, he wants a presence that supports the army, monitors the ground and helps residents return [8].
On the morning of Tuesday, November 24, Lebanese media reported Israeli strikes and explosions in the buffer zone held by Israel in southern Lebanon, including in Mayfadoun and Kfar Tebnit [7].
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, said Israel wants to leave Lebanon but cannot as long as Hezbollah remains a threat [7].

Key takeaway: from January 1, UN peacekeepers begin to leave, and no force is planned to replace them along the border with Israel. Europeans are offering training north of the Litani, not soldiers on the border [1][2][4].

France and Italy want to set up a multinational "coalition" to take over, but nothing has been decided. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in October she preferred a new UN mandate [4]. The European mission can only go south of the Litani with Beirut's consent and if security allows [1][2].

The framework negotiated on June 26 under US auspices provides for an Israeli withdrawal, the disarmament of Hezbollah and the deployment of the Lebanese army starting from two pilot zones. But talks with Israel are suspended pending the formation of a new Israeli government [8].
On November 21, Independence Day, Joseph Aoun denounced both "the Israeli occupation of part of our land" and interference by "certain influential parties in the Iranian regime" [6].

Paris is on the front line to avoid a vacuum in southern Lebanon: Jean-Noël Barrot visited Beirut in October and says he wants to keep a French presence after UNIFIL, if Lebanon asks for it. A southern Lebanon without a referee would raise the risk of a new war, in a region already under strain.

Livret A: French savers withdraw another €2.62 billion in October, the worst ten months since 2008

The Livret A savings account lost €2.62 billion in October 2026, its eighth straight month of net withdrawals, according to Caisse des dépôts figures published on Tuesday, November 24. Since January, €9.54 billion has flowed out, a level unseen since 2008, because inflation (3.4%) is well above the account's rate (1.7%) [1][4][5].
In October, French savers withdrew €2.62 billion more than they deposited in their Livret A accounts, according to the Caisse des dépôts, which manages the money collected [1][4].
It is the eighth consecutive month of net outflows, meaning withdrawals exceeded deposits [1][3]. The record remains October 2025, with €3.81 billion in net withdrawals [4][5].
The Livret de développement durable et solidaire (LDDS), the other regulated savings account, lost €940 million over the month [1].
Over the first ten months of the year, the Livret A lost €9.54 billion: you have to go back to 2008 to find worse [4][5]. In September, €1.52 billion had already left the account [7].
Total deposits, meaning all the money held in Livret A accounts, remain huge: €440.1 billion at the end of October [1].
October is usually a month of withdrawals, as households pay property tax and the balance of their income tax [3][4].
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on November 3 that the Livret A ceiling, currently €22,950, will rise to between €25,000 and €30,000 on February 1, 2027 [6].
Key takeaway: French households are dipping into their rainy-day savings because their purchasing power is being squeezed, and because the Livret A earns less than the rise in prices [1][5].

With inflation at 3.4% and a rate of 1.7%, money held in a Livret A loses real value every month: €100 deposited at the start of the year is worth less by the end [1][5]. Some savers are therefore looking for better returns elsewhere, while others simply need to pay their bills.

The government chose to raise the ceiling to attract new deposits, a decision taken by decree, without a vote in Parliament [6]. But the measure changes nothing for the vast majority of savers, whose accounts are far from full: it is rising prices and the low rate that are driving money away [5][6].

Morale is following the same downward path: Insee's household confidence indicator fell to 80 in October, its lowest level since June 2013, against a long-term average of 100 [8][9]. The November figure is published this Wednesday, November 25.

If your Livret A is sitting with a few thousand euros in it, know that it currently earns less than the rise in prices: it protects your money from risk, not from inflation. Keep your emergency savings there, and look at the new rate and new ceiling announced for February 1.

China: Shanghai Party chief Chen Jining under anti-corruption investigation, the fourth Politburo member to fall since 2022

On Tuesday, November 24, Beijing announced an investigation into Chen Jining, Communist Party secretary of Shanghai and a member of the Politburo, for "serious violations of discipline and law". Seen as a frontrunner to enter the top tier of power in 2027, he is the fourth member of this body targeted since 2022 [1][3][4].

The announcement came from the official Xinhua news agency and state broadcaster CCTV: the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the Party's internal police, is investigating Chen Jining [1][3][5].
In official Chinese language, the phrase "serious violations of discipline and law" refers to suspected corruption. The announcement gave no further details [2][3].

Chen Jining has led the Party in Shanghai since 2022, after five years as mayor of Beijing [3]. He succeeded Li Qiang there, a promotion seen at the time as a "surprise", as he had no experience of the city [7].
He is the fourth of the 24 Politburo members appointed in 2022 to be targeted, after generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, and Ma Xingrui [1].
According to Al Jazeera, he is the first Shanghai Party chief to be investigated in two decades [1]. His predecessor Chen Liangyu was dismissed in 2006 [9].
A former environment minister who came through Tsinghua University, Xi Jinping's alma mater, he was regarded as loyal to the Chinese president [7].

Key takeaway: the purge launched by Xi Jinping now reaches the circle of future leaders. Chen Jining was seen as a serious candidate for the Politburo Standing Committee, the supreme body of power, and the investigation surprised analysts [4].
The timing matters: the 21st Party Congress, which will renew the leadership, is due to be held in Beijing in the second half of 2027 [3]. Each fall reshuffles the deck for the succession.

The series is unprecedented. He Weidong, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, was expelled from the Party in October 2025, and Zhang Youxia, the army's highest-ranking officer, has been under investigation since January [6]. Ma Xingrui was expelled in July and sent to trial for corruption [6][10]. The Journal of Democracy sees it as the biggest upheaval at the top of Chinese power since the 1970s [8].

Shanghai is one of the main gateways for foreign companies into China. Unstable political leadership can delay economic decisions or approvals. If you work with China or your savings are exposed to it, this is a signal to watch ahead of the 2027 congress.
